'''''Syntrichia ruralis''''', commonly known as '''twisted moss''' and '''star moss''',<ref name=matt>Matthews, Robin F. 1993. [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/bryophyte/torrur/all.html ''Tortula ruralis''.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory (Producer).</ref> is a species of [[moss]] in the family [[Pottiaceae]] with a [[cosmopolitan distribution]]. It occurs in North America, the Pacific, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, North and South Africa, South America, and Australia. It grows in many types of [[climate]], including the [[Arctic]], [[boreal ecosystem|boreal]] areas, [[Temperateness|temperate]] areas, and [[desert]]s. It grows in [[tundra]], [[coniferous forest]], [[grassland]], [[sagebrush steppe]], and other habitat types.<ref name=matt/>

This moss forms tufts of erect stems up to 4 centimeters tall. When it is wet it is bright green and the leaves are loose. When it dries the leaves wrap around the stem and it becomes reddish brown in color. It is [[dioecious]]. It also performs [[vegetative reproduction]].<ref name=matt/>

Though it occurs in many types of habitat, it is usually not a [[Dominance (ecology)|dominant species]]. The moss grows on many types of soil, but most often [[calcium|calcareous]] soils. It tolerates a variety of [[elevation]]s and levels of sunlight. It may be a component in [[Cryptobiotic soil|cryptogamic crusts]]. It helps to stabilize soil and reduce [[erosion]]. It can dry out and become dormant for many years, becoming metabolically active again after many decades of [[desiccation]].<ref name=matt/> It is used as a [[model organism]] in studies of desiccation.<ref name=oliver>Oliver, M. J. (2010). [http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2164/11/143 Chloroplast genome sequence of the moss ''Tortula ruralis'': Gene content, polymorphism, and structural arrangement relative to other green plant chloroplast genomes.] ''BMC Genomics'' 11 143.</ref> Within one hour of rehydration it is making new proteins and within two hours it is performing [[photosynthesis]].<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.killerplants.com/weird-plants/20020725.asp |last=Vandaveer | first= Chelsie | title= Why is Star Moss Strange? |  date= July 25, 2002 | access-date= December 14, 2004 }}</ref>
